Passage 1: A compiler parses source code into a syntax tree, checks types, and lowers expressions into an intermediate representation. Register allocation and instruction scheduling depend on the target architecture.

Passage 2: A distributed database partitions records across servers. Replication improves availability, while consensus determines which updates become committed. Transaction isolation defines what concurrent readers can observe.

Passage 3: A laboratory team measures enzyme activity at several temperatures. Controls are repeated, calibration errors are recorded, and conclusions distinguish correlation from causation.

Passage 4: An observatory records spectra from distant stars. Spectral lines reveal chemical composition, while changes in wavelength can indicate relative motion. Instrument resolution limits interpretation.

Passage 5: A warehouse schedules deliveries using capacity constraints and arrival windows. The planner compares total travel distance, late deliveries, and idle vehicles before choosing a route.

Passage 6: A numerical simulation solves a system of differential equations on a grid. Boundary conditions, time step selection, discretization error, and convergence tests determine the reliability of the result.

Passage 7: An image processing pipeline corrects sensor noise and measures edges. A convolution applies the same filter at every spatial position. Resampling changes resolution but cannot recover missing information.

Passage 8: An operating system maps virtual addresses to physical pages. Page faults, filesystem caches, memory pressure, and storage latency can all influence application startup time.

Passage 9: A network transmits packets through switches with finite buffers. Congestion control balances throughput and latency. End-to-end measurements include queueing and application processing overhead.

Passage 10: A software team reviews a change to an API. Tests cover invalid inputs, concurrency, and backward compatibility. Logs retain request identifiers so failures can be traced across services.

Passage 11: A matrix multiplication computes C[i,j] as the sum of A[i,k] times B[k,j]. Tiling improves reuse, but useful tile sizes depend on dimensions, precision, alignment, and available memory.

Passage 12: An engineer compares inference architectures using measured timelines. Independent operations may overlap, so adding individual kernel durations does not necessarily reproduce wall-clock latency.
